# Reflection — STAR, cycle #19

> **Note:** This feedback is AI-generated. It's observational, not authoritative. Use what's useful.

Vibe Cartographer cycle #19, 2026-08-10. Mode: fully-autonomous (*Autonomous — Self*).
Persona: Architect. Onboard through checklist and a twelve-item build, in one day.

Cycle #19 extended a shipped Pipeline A with three things: Google account linking that adds
rather than replaces, Pipeline B (Script Check), and an HTTPS MCP server making the same
department callable by an agent. All three shipped. 473 tests, `ruff` at 0, deployed and
verified in production at `star.626labs.dev`.

## Scope & Idea Clarity

**What landed:** The narrowing, and it is the strongest single decision in the cycle.
`/onboard` stated the goal as "replace anonymous Firebase auth with `GoogleAuthProvider`."
`scope.md` refused it and argued the refusal, citing the close-the-tab moment at
`critique-adversarial.md:9` and the rebuttal `DIRECTION.md:54` already recorded. Google
became an *upgrade on* the anonymous session rather than a replacement for it. That one call
is why the intake path from landing to a filed room still contains zero mentions of accounts,
a criterion the build tested and passed. Turning a stated requirement into an argument, and
winning, is what a scope document is for.

**What to tighten:** Three users are named — the screenwriter, the agent, and the builder
running personas — but only one got criteria that test its own experience. The agent's
surface is measured down to individual error strings. The screenwriter's requirement, "cycle
#19 must not cost this user anything," is asserted and never measured. The adversarial-persona
plan is exactly the instrument that closes it, and it belongs in scope as a deliverable rather
than arriving after ship.

## Requirements Thinking

**What landed:** Nine forks closed with their reasoning attached and "a one-line edit to
override" on each. That is what let `/spec` and `/build` proceed without re-litigating
anything already decided. Decision #8 is the standout: choosing a full-page OIDC redirect over
Google Identity Services because GIS is a remote `<script>`, and a remote script is the silent
mid-demo failure the zero-third-party rule exists to prevent. A security call wearing an
implementation detail's clothes, and it held under live fire.

**What to tighten:** Zero deepening rounds, consistent with the standing pattern, and the one
requirement the PRD missed is the one a second pass most plausibly catches. The document
discusses anonymous identity for pages without ever asking what happens to a writer's work
when the session that owns it is gone. A round would not certainly have found it — but "what
does this user lose, and how" is the question a second pass exists to ask.

## Technical Decisions

**What landed:** Decision 1, hand-writing the MCP transport against the spec rather than
adding the SDK, with four reasons in descending weight. The fourth is the one worth keeping:
the `mcp` package is MIT, publishes no model calls, and is clearly allowed on the merits — but
its maintainer address would make an argument a judge has to be walked through, and *not having
the line in `pyproject.toml` is worth more than winning that argument*. That is judgment about
a judging process rather than about engineering, and it is the kind of call a spec usually
cannot make. It paid twice: no dependency risk on a fresh Cloud Build, and the packaging line
proved out in production.

**What to tighten:** The room-payload estimate. `spec.md > Open issues` #5 put a room at
11,000-17,000 characters. Measured over the wire during the harness runs: **152,007 bytes**,
roughly 37,000 tokens — an order of magnitude out, and in the wrong place, since the bible is
only 16,183 of it and the drawers are 127,090. It is the one number in the document that was
guessed while it was measurable: a stored room existed at spec time. Numbers that later
decisions rest on are worth the five minutes.

## Plan vs. Reality

**What landed:** The checklist was never revised. Twelve items, four gates, the sequence
intact from first to last, and the "When Something Breaks" protocol never invoked. The
artifact drift confirms it independently — 0% on `scope.md` and `prd.md`, 1% on `spec.md`,
9% on `checklist.md` and nearly all of that is checkboxes. Across a build touching more than
forty files, that is a plan holding rather than one quietly re-cut to match what happened.

One deviation, taken deliberately: item 1 was a browser-and-console step only the builder
could run, and its failure reshaped items 2-4 and nothing else, so Gate B ran in parallel
rather than idling behind it. Item 1 still landed before a line of Gate A code was written,
which is the whole of the ordering argument `/checklist` made.

**What to tighten:** The plan had no slot for the defect class that actually dominated. Three
shipped sentences turned out to be false: `.env.example` crediting "Firestore rules" this
project deliberately does not deploy, the README claiming STAR "verifies" claims in the first
paragraph a judge reads, and the intake's "nothing is visible without your sign-in token,"
which a long-lived MCP credential makes untrue. Phase 3 found the same class and named it —
"copy and comments claiming more than the code could support." It keeps recurring and keeps
being caught by accident. A copy audit deserves its own checklist line, the way the security
sweep has one.

## How You Worked

**What landed:** Decisions made at the right altitude. Offered a recommendation and its
reasoning on the check rate-limit gap, the answer was "close it at item 10" — four words, no
re-derivation of a tradeoff already laid out, and it shaped how item 10 was built. The same
posture appears on the multi-point answers throughout: "1 I need a room. 2 close it at item
10. 3 ok. Dispatch 9 now." Four decisions, one message, no ceremony.

The sharpest contribution came after everything was green and deployed: pushing on whether a
user who never signed in can recover their work. That reopened a premise the whole cycle
rested on, at the least comfortable moment to raise it, and it was right — seven rooms were
stranded across six anonymous sessions, and the design had no recovery path by construction.

**What to tighten:** Two decision requests evaporated in traffic. Half of that is the agent's
fault for burying asks at the bottom of status reports, but the posture fix at this scale is
to name a batching protocol at kickoff: hold non-blocking calls for the checkpoint, interrupt
for blocking ones. Twelve parallel agents generate more decisions than a linear build, and the
ones that do not block get lost by default.

## Your Goals

The stated outcome was a submission that survives Stage One and scores on Stage Two.

**Stage One is mechanically clear.** MIT license present and detected. `google-adk` /
`google-genai` and `parallel-web` are imported *and called at runtime* in **both** pipelines,
verified live rather than asserted — Pipeline B's first real run reported `search_count: 1`
and the harness runs spent ten more.

**Stage Two is strongest where the work is deepest.** Implementation has a ledger-backed
provenance model most entries will not have: a model authors the verdict and never a title, an
excerpt, or a claim about where something came from. Design has a direction that measures
itself — manila's share of the filed room is computed from union area at five widths rather
than judged by eye.

**Impact is the thin axis**, and thin for the reason the builder named: the screenwriter's
experience is the one nobody adversarially tested. The instrument for that already exists in
the repo — `harness/` drives Gemini personas against the live surface and commits the
transcripts — and the voice already exists in `docs/design/critique-adversarial.md`. Pointing
the second at the first is the highest-value next move.

## Reflection

Asked what surprised him, the builder said: *"Nothing. This process works."* On cycle nineteen
that is the correct answer and worth recording as-is.

Asked whether the three goals landed, he put it at **99.8%** — the missing fraction being that
the MCP server is not yet connected from a desktop client. Worth stating precisely, because it
is not a build failure. The goal as scoped was an HTTPS MCP server with per-user bearer tokens
and the **OAuth 2.1 authorization server explicitly deferred**, and that shipped complete. The
missing 0.2% is that deferral being felt for the first time: a desktop client's connector flow
begins by asking where the authorization server is, and STAR answers 404 four different ways.
At scope time the cut read as free, and it was free against the judging criteria. It was not
free against the experience, and that only became visible by reaching for the thing. It is
better carried as "the cut to un-cut first" than as a fraction missing.

One thing surprised the agent, recorded as the agent's own. During the persona runs a bug in
the harness's spend guard charged a refused call against its budget, starving a persona of the
tool it needed. Denied the tool, the model wrote five confident verdicts straight off the
research bible — three contradicting the real check — under headings reading "Research Bible
Grounding." That is the exact failure mode the entire ledger architecture exists to refuse,
reproduced in a single turn, by the same class of model the pipeline runs on. Nobody designed
that test. A defect in budget accounting ran it, and it is the most persuasive argument for
this product's design that the cycle produced.

## What the process caught, and what it did not

Six defects, none of them found by tests passing:

1. A search budget that inverted at its safest setting — `STAR_MAX_SEARCHES_PER_CHECK=0`
   handed a run the build's 30.
2. An anchor matcher silently losing a mark, found by mutation-testing a suite that had passed
   on its first run.
3. A `ReferenceError` that took the whole docket down on a partial room, shipped and invisible
   to every complete run.
4. A verifier answering from memory, spending 1 of 8 searches and leaving the scene's most
   obvious anachronism unstamped.
5. An off-story scene reading as a clean pass, found by a persona.
6. The harness's own spend guard, above.

Three false claims in shipped copy, and one false claim in the agent's own route audit, which
reported the SSE stream as `_require_uid`-guarded by matching a docstring rather than the code.

**The pattern worth carrying forward:** every defect the process caught is of the form *the
code does not do what we said*. The two things it missed are both of the form *what we said
does not serve the user* — the recovery gap, and Cloud Run serving four hostnames where every
artifact named one. The builder's own diagnosis is the right one: that blindness scales with
domain distance. On familiar ground the builder's instincts stand where that check belongs; on
unfamiliar ground nothing does, and the artifacts specify the wrong thing in great detail.
